title: Dark blood, chest pain, rising potassium
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: At 8:30 a.m., Mrs. Linda Ocampo, 61, at Station 9 reports back and chest pain and nausea. The blood in her venous line looks translucent, like red wine. Two minutes later, the patient at Station 10 says his back hurts.

n1.prompt: What do you do at Station 9?

choices.text: Stop the pump, clamp, do not return the blood; urgent potassium; call the physician.
choices.feedback: Hemolyzed blood carries potassium and is never returned. Monitor him and send hemoglobin with the potassium.

choices.text: Return the blood and end the session, so he does not lose the blood in the circuit.

n2.scene: Station 10 has the same symptoms; his venous line also looks abnormal.
n2.prompt: What does the charge nurse do?

choices.text: Declare a possible cluster: clamp Station 10, check everyone on the same water, hold new starts.
choices.feedback: Hemolysis is often a shared supply fault. Call the Medical Director; the technician keeps the lines and samples the water and fluid.

choices.text: Treat Station 10 separately later, once Station 9 is stable, since two cases may be a coincidence.
choices.feedback: A cluster needs immediate action across the unit.
choices.then: You declare the cluster five minutes later.

n3.scene: Mrs. Ocampo’s potassium is 7.4 mmol/L; the ECG shows peaked T waves. At 8:55 she becomes unresponsive and pulseless.

choices.text: Arrest algorithm with potassium treatment; blood not returned; the watcher covers the rest.
choices.feedback: Potassium is the reversible cause; the circuit decision stays. The watcher covers Station 10 and every other patient.

choices.text: Everyone goes to Station 9, since a cardiac arrest needs every pair of hands in the unit.
choices.feedback: Station 10 is also affected and needs a watcher.
choices.then: The charge nurse sends one nurse back to Station 10.

end.title: 10:00 a.m.
end.text: Mrs. Ocampo has ROSC and is transferred; the patient at Station 10 is stable. The water team finds a carbon tank breakthrough. No treatment restarts until the water and fluid are cleared.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Port-wine blood is never returned.
  • One hemolysis can be a cluster: check everyone on the same supply.
  • Potassium drives the arrest risk; keep a watcher for the other patients.
